decks.title: Skeleton: Movement and Locomotion — Part 1: Functions of the skeleton, axial and appendicular parts
goals: List the functions of the human skeleton
Name the parts of the axial and the appendicular skeleton
Classify named bones as axial or appendicular

slides.heading: The Human Skeleton
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what the bones do, and how the skeleton is organised.

visual.alt: Flow from bones joined together to the skeleton and its functions

slides.narration: Without a skeleton your body would be a soft heap. Your bones are joined together to form a framework that holds you up, guards soft organs and lets you move. In this part we look at what the skeleton does and how it is organised.

slides.heading: Functions of the skeleton

rows: Gives the body its upright shape and holds it up
Skull guards the brain; ribs guard the heart and lungs; vertebral column guards the spinal cord
Muscles pull on bones, which act as levers
Bones give firm places for muscles to attach
Red bone marrow makes red and white blood cells

visual.alt: Table of six functions of the human skeleton with examples

slides.narration: The skeleton supports the body and gives it shape. It protects soft organs. It allows movement because muscles pull on bones. The red bone marrow makes blood cells, and the bones store calcium and phosphorus.

slides.heading: Who guards what
slides.body_md: The **cranium** is a rigid box; the **ribs** form a cage; the **vertebrae** form a canal around the cord.

visual.alt: Table of the bones that protect the brain, the heart and lungs, and the spinal cord

slides.narration: Three groups of bones act as armour. The skull is a hard box around the brain. The ribs and breastbone form a cage around the heart and lungs. The vertebrae are stacked to form a tunnel that guards the spinal cord.

slides.heading: Axial and appendicular skeleton
slides.body_md: The **axial** skeleton forms the main axis of the body; the **appendicular** skeleton forms the limbs and their girdles.

slides.narration: The skeleton is divided into two parts. The axial skeleton lies along the middle line of the body and has the skull, the vertebral column, the ribs and the breastbone. The appendicular skeleton has the limb bones and the girdles that join them to the axis.

slides.heading: The axial skeleton

rows: Neck, chest, lower back, sacrum, coccyx
33 in a child; 26 in an adult

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the axial skeleton and the number of bones in each

slides.narration: The axial skeleton has the skull, made of cranial and facial bones. It has the vertebral column, twelve pairs of ribs and the sternum. Many books also count the hyoid bone and the small bones of the ears. Together they make about eighty bones in an adult.

slides.heading: The vertebral column
slides.body_md: 7 + 12 + 5 movable vertebrae, then the **sacrum** and the **coccyx**, where vertebrae have fused.

slides.narration: The vertebral column has five regions. Seven cervical vertebrae are in the neck, twelve thoracic vertebrae carry the ribs, and five lumbar vertebrae are in the lower back. Then come the sacrum and the coccyx, each formed by vertebrae that fuse together as a child grows.

slides.heading: Quick check: an axial bone
slides.body_md: Which of these bones belongs to the axial skeleton?
slides.narration: It lies in the middle of the chest.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting the axial skeleton
slides.body_md: Find the number of bones in the axial skeleton of an adult from its parts.
bullets: Step 1: skull 8 + 14 = **22**; hyoid **1**; ear bones 3 × 2 = **6**.
Step 2: vertebral column 24 movable + 1 sacrum + 1 coccyx = **26**; sternum **1**; ribs 12 × 2 = **24**.

visual.alt: Worked table adding twenty-two, one, six, twenty-six, one and twenty-four to give eighty

slides.narration: Add the parts one by one. The skull has twenty-two bones, the hyoid one, the ear bones six, the vertebral column twenty-six, the sternum one and the ribs twenty-four. The total is eighty bones.

slides.heading: The appendicular skeleton

rows: Clavicle and scapula, on each side
Humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges
Femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the appendicular skeleton and the number of bones in each

slides.narration: The appendicular skeleton has two girdles and four limbs. The pectoral girdle at the shoulder has a clavicle and a scapula on each side. The pelvic girdle has two hip bones. Each upper limb and each lower limb has thirty bones.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting the appendicular skeleton
slides.body_md: Add the bones of the girdles and the four limbs, and then find the bones in the whole adult skeleton.
bullets: Step 1: pectoral girdle = 2 + 2 = **4**; pelvic girdle = **2**.
Step 3: appendicular = 4 + 2 + 120 = **126**; whole skeleton = 80 + 126 = **206**.

visual.alt: Worked table giving one hundred twenty-six appendicular bones and two hundred six in all

slides.narration: The girdles have six bones, and the four limbs have one hundred twenty. That is one hundred twenty-six bones in the appendicular skeleton. Add the eighty bones of the axial skeleton and an adult has two hundred six bones.

slides.heading: Quick check: a limb bone
slides.narration: Think of the arm.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: sorting named bones
slides.body_md: Classify each bone as axial or appendicular: skull, humerus, sternum, femur, scapula, rib, vertebra, hip bone.
bullets: Step 1: bones on the **middle line** or in the **head and trunk case** are axial.
Step 2: bones of the **limbs** and the **girdles** that carry them are appendicular.
Step 3: sort the list using these two rules.

visual.alt: Worked table sorting eight bones into four axial and four appendicular

slides.narration: Use two rules. Bones of the head, the chest and the backbone are axial. Bones of the limbs, and the shoulder and hip girdles that hold them, are appendicular. So the skull, sternum, rib and vertebra are axial, and the other four are appendicular.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: The skeleton supports, protects, helps movement, makes blood cells and stores minerals.
Axial: skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum.
Appendicular: pectoral girdle, pelvic girdle and the limb bones.

rows: Girdles and the bones of the limbs

visual.alt: Summary table of the axial and appendicular skeleton

slides.narration: To recap. The skeleton has six main jobs: support, protection, movement, muscle attachment, making blood cells and storing minerals. The axial skeleton is the skull, backbone, ribs and sternum. The appendicular skeleton is the girdles and limbs.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give functions as **short separate points**, with an example of each.
Say that the **skull protects the brain**, the **rib cage the heart and lungs**, the **vertebral column the spinal cord**.
**Girdles belong to the appendicular skeleton**, not to the axial one.
In a labelled sketch, name the **clavicle, scapula, humerus** and **femur** correctly.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write the functions as short separate points with an example. Match each protective bone with the organ it guards. Remember that the girdles belong to the appendicular skeleton. And spell the limb bones correctly in a labelled sketch.

slides.heading: Joints
slides.body_md: Part 2 — where bones meet and how that decides how we move.

visual.alt: Flow from two bones meeting to a joint and to the type of movement

slides.narration: A joint is a place where two or more bones meet. The kind of joint decides how much the bones can move. Some joints do not move at all, some move a little, and some move freely in different ways.

slides.heading: Three kinds of joints

rows: Between the bones of the skull
Between the vertebrae; the pubic joint of the pelvis
Shoulder, elbow, hip, knee, wrist, ankle, neck

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of joints with their movement and where each is found

slides.narration: Joints are grouped into three kinds. Immovable joints, such as those between skull bones, do not move. Slightly movable joints, such as those between the vertebrae, move a little. Freely movable joints, such as the shoulder and knee, move through a wide range.

slides.heading: Immovable joints

rows: Between the bones of the cranium (and the face)
None; the edges of the bones interlock
Keeps the skull a strong, rigid box that protects the brain

visual.alt: Table giving the location, movement and use of immovable joints

slides.narration: The bones of the skull are held together by joints that cannot move. The edges of the bones interlock like pieces of a jigsaw. This keeps the skull a rigid box, which is just what is needed to protect the brain.

slides.heading: Quick check: joints of the skull
slides.body_md: The joints between the bones of the cranium are
slides.narration: Think of what the skull has to do.

slides.heading: Slightly movable joints

rows: Between neighbouring vertebrae; the front of the pelvis
A little; the bones are joined by pads of cartilage
Lets the backbone bend and twist a little, and absorbs shocks

visual.alt: Table giving the location, movement and use of slightly movable joints

slides.narration: Between two vertebrae lies a pad of cartilage. It lets each vertebra move only a little. But with twenty-four movable vertebrae together, the backbone can bend and twist, and the pads also soften the shock of walking and jumping.

slides.heading: Freely movable joints
slides.body_md: Most freely movable joints are enclosed in a capsule containing **synovial fluid**.

rows: Oily fluid that lubricates the joint
Strong bands that hold the bones together

visual.alt: Table of three parts common to freely movable joints and the job of each

slides.narration: Freely movable joints have smooth cartilage on the bone ends and a lubricating fluid inside a capsule. Strong bands called ligaments hold the bones together. There are four main kinds: ball and socket, hinge, gliding and pivot.

slides.heading: Four freely movable joints
slides.body_md: The shape of the joint decides the movement.

slides.narration: In a ball and socket joint, a rounded end fits into a cup, so the bone can move in all directions. A hinge joint swings in one plane only, like a door. In a pivot joint, one bone turns around another. In a gliding joint, flat surfaces slide over each other.

Rotation of one bone round another

slides.narration: The shoulder and the hip are ball and socket joints and allow the widest movement. The elbow and knee are hinge joints and bend in one plane. The joint between the first two neck bones is a pivot. The wrist and ankle have gliding joints.

slides.body_md: A joint that moves back and forth like a door on its hinges is found at the
slides.narration: Think of bending the arm.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which joint does the action?
slides.body_md: Name the joint that allows each action: swinging the arm in a full circle, bending the knee, shaking the head to say no, and sliding the wrist bones when you write.
bullets: Step 1: a full circle needs movement in **all directions**: **ball and socket**, at the shoulder.
Step 2: bending in one plane is a **hinge**, at the knee.
Step 3: turning the head is **rotation** of one bone on another: **pivot**, between the atlas and axis.
Step 4: small slides are **gliding**, at the wrist.

rows: Swing the arm in a circle

visual.alt: Worked table matching four actions with ball and socket, hinge, pivot and gliding joints

slides.narration: Ask what kind of movement the action needs. A full circle needs all directions, so ball and socket. Bending one way and back is a hinge. Turning is a pivot. Tiny slides are a gliding joint.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sorting a list of joints
slides.body_md: A student lists eight joints. Count how many are immovable, slightly movable and freely movable, and how many of the freely movable ones are hinge or ball and socket.
bullets: Step 1: the suture between skull bones is **immovable** (1); the joint between two vertebrae is **slightly movable** (1).
Step 2: the other six are **freely movable** (6).
Step 3: shoulder and hip are **ball and socket** (2); elbow and knee are **hinge** (2); the wrist and the atlas-axis joint are the other two.

visual.alt: Worked table of eight joints with their kind

slides.narration: Sort the list. The skull suture does not move and the joint between vertebrae moves a little. The other six are freely movable. Of those, two are ball and socket, two are hinge, and one each are gliding and pivot.

slides.body_md: Turning the head to say no happens mainly at a
slides.narration: One bone turns round the peg of another.

slides.heading: Why have different kinds of joints?

rows: Allows the movements needed for locomotion and work

visual.alt: Table giving the advantage of immovable, slightly movable and freely movable joints

slides.narration: Each kind of joint suits a job. Immovable joints make a strong box for the brain. Slightly movable joints make the backbone flexible and absorb shocks. Freely movable joints let us walk, run, throw and write.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Three kinds: immovable (skull), slightly movable (vertebrae) and freely movable.
Freely movable: ball and socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (elbow, knee), pivot (atlas on axis), gliding (wrist, ankle).
Cartilage, synovial fluid and ligaments make freely movable joints smooth and strong.

visual.alt: Summary table of four freely movable joints with an example of each

slides.narration: To recap. Joints may be immovable, slightly movable or freely movable. The four freely movable kinds are ball and socket, hinge, pivot and gliding, and each has its own examples in the body.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always give a **location** with the joint.
Describe the **movement** in a few words: **all directions**, **one plane**, **rotation**, **sliding**.
The **skull** joints are **immovable**; the joints between **vertebrae** are **slightly movable**.
Do not say the **knee** is a ball and socket joint: it is a **hinge**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give a place for every joint. Describe the movement in a few words, such as all directions, one plane, rotation or sliding. Skull joints are immovable, and the joints between vertebrae move a little. The knee is a hinge, not a ball and socket.

notes.title: Skeleton: Movement and Locomotion — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Functions of the human skeleton
sections.body_md:
The **skeleton** is the framework of bones, cartilage and joints. Its functions are:

1. **Support and shape:** it holds the body up and gives it its shape.
2. **Protection:** the **skull** protects the brain; the **rib cage** (ribs and sternum) protects the heart and lungs; the **vertebral column** protects the spinal cord.
3. **Movement and locomotion:** muscles pull on bones across joints, so the bones act as levers.
4. **Attachment of muscles:** bones give firm places for muscles to be fixed by tendons.
5. **Making blood cells:** red bone marrow in some bones makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
6. **Storage of minerals:** bones store **calcium** and **phosphorus** and release them when the body needs them.

Bones are living tissue: they grow, repair themselves and carry blood vessels. Books may add that the small bones of the middle ear carry sound and that yellow marrow stores fat; the six points above are the core.

key_terms.definition_md: The framework of bones that supports the body.
The soft tissue inside some bones that makes blood cells.
A strong cord that joins a muscle to a bone.

sections.heading: 2. Axial and appendicular skeleton
sections.body_md:
The adult skeleton has about **206** bones, in two parts.

**Axial skeleton** (lies along the axis of the body; about 80 bones):
- **Skull:** 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones.
- **Vertebral column:** 7 **cervical** (neck), 12 **thoracic** (chest, carrying ribs), 5 **lumbar** (lower back), 5 **sacral** (fused into the **sacrum**) and 4 **coccygeal** (fused into the **coccyx**): 33 vertebrae in a child, 26 bones in an adult.
- **Ribs:** 12 pairs (7 pairs **true ribs** joined to the sternum, 3 pairs **false ribs**, 2 pairs **floating ribs**).
- **Sternum** (breastbone): 1.
- Many books also place the **hyoid** (1) and the small **ear bones** (6) here.

**Appendicular skeleton** (limbs and girdles; about 126 bones):
- **Pectoral girdle:** a clavicle (collar bone) and a scapula (shoulder blade) on each side.
- **Upper limb** (30 each): humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges.
- **Pelvic girdle:** 2 hip bones (joined to the sacrum).
- **Lower limb** (30 each): femur, patella (knee cap), tibia, fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges.

Counts differ a little between books (for example, whether the hyoid and ear bones are counted, and a child has more bones than an adult because some fuse); the totals 206, 80 and 126 are the usual ones.

key_terms.definition_md: Skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum.
The bones of the limbs and of the girdles that join them to the axial skeleton.
A ring of bones that attaches a limb to the axial skeleton.

sections.heading: 3. Joints
sections.body_md:
A **joint** is a place where two or more bones meet.

| Kind | Movement | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Immovable (fixed)** | None | Between the bones of the skull (sutures) |
| **Slightly movable** | A little | Between the vertebrae; the pubic joint at the front of the pelvis |
| **Freely movable** | Wide | Shoulder, elbow, hip, knee, wrist, ankle, neck |

**Types of freely movable joints**

| Type | Movement | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Ball and socket** | In all directions, and rotation | Shoulder, hip |
| **Hinge** | Back and forth in one plane, like a door | Elbow, knee, joints of the fingers and toes |
| **Pivot** | One bone turns round another | Atlas on axis in the neck (turning the head) |
| **Gliding** | Small sliding movements | Wrist (between carpals), ankle (between tarsals) |

Most freely movable joints are enclosed in a capsule with **synovial fluid**, have **cartilage** on the bone ends and are held by **ligaments**.

The shoulder, with its shallow socket, moves most widely; the hip, with a deeper socket, is more stable. Books also describe other types (saddle, condyloid), which are not part of this chapter.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Listing the **girdles** under the axial skeleton; they belong to the **appendicular** skeleton.
- Saying the knee or elbow is a **ball and socket** joint; both are **hinge** joints.
- Writing the skull as a **freely movable** joint; its joints are **immovable**.
- Giving a joint without its **location**, or movement without naming the **type**.
- Writing **single words** for functions with no example.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an odd one out **with its category**, a give-reason item.
- 2 marks: two functions or two points, matched.
- 3 marks: three differences between joints, or three functions with examples.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation or diagram with parts of 2 to 4 marks; one part is a labelled diagram.

questions.stem_md: State (i) where blood cells are made in the skeleton and (ii) the two minerals stored in bones.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Blood cells are made in the **red bone marrow** of some bones. (ii) Bones store **calcium** and **phosphorus**, which make them hard and strong.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the skeleton helps the body to move.

questions.stem_md: State three functions of the human skeleton and give one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Support**: it holds the body upright and gives it its shape.
2. **Protection**: the skull protects the brain (or the rib cage the heart and lungs).

The vertebral column has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae that remain separate. How many vertebrae are separate (movable) in all?

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Axial skeleton | Appendicular skeleton |
|---|---|
| Lies along the **axis** of the body | Forms the **limbs** and their **girdles** |
| Skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum | Clavicle, scapula, hip bones and limb bones |
| About **80** bones in an adult | About **126** bones in an adult |
| Mainly **protects** organs and supports the body | Mainly helps **movement** |

questions.solution_md: A suture is an immovable joint.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the backbone can bend and twist although each joint between two vertebrae moves only a little.

answer.model_answer_md: There are many (**twenty-four**) movable vertebrae, so the **small movements add up**.

questions.solution_md: Many small movements add up.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the fluid that lubricates a freely movable joint.

answer.model_answer_md: **Synovial fluid.**

questions.solution_md: Synovial fluid.

questions.stem_md: Name the kind of joint found between the bones of the skull and state its use.

answer.model_answer_md: The skull bones are held by **immovable (fixed) joints**. They keep the skull a **rigid box** that protects the brain.

questions.solution_md: Immovable; keeps the skull rigid to protect the brain.

marking_scheme.step: Keeps skull rigid to protect the brain

questions.stem_md: Name the kind of joint between two vertebrae and state one advantage of such a joint.

answer.model_answer_md: A **slightly movable joint**, in which the bones are joined by a pad of cartilage. It lets the backbone **bend a little** and the pad **absorbs shocks** when we walk or jump.

questions.solution_md: Slightly movable; flexibility or shock absorption.

questions.stem_md: Name the joint that lets you shake your head to say no, and name the two bones that form it.

answer.model_answer_md: A **pivot joint**, formed by the **atlas** (first vertebra), which turns on the **axis** (second vertebra).

questions.solution_md: Pivot joint; atlas and axis.

questions.stem_md: State two features of a freely movable joint that make it smooth and strong.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cartilage** and **synovial fluid** make the bone ends smooth and reduce friction. **Ligaments** hold the bones together.

questions.solution_md: Cartilage and synovial fluid; ligaments.

marking_scheme.step: Cartilage or synovial fluid for smoothness

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between a ball and socket joint and a hinge joint.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Ball and socket joint | Hinge joint |
|---|---|
| Movement in **all directions** and rotation | Movement in **one plane** only |
| A rounded end fits into a **cup** | Bones joined by a **pin-like** arrangement, like a door |
| **Shoulder, hip** | **Elbow, knee** |

questions.solution_md: Movement; structure; location.

questions.stem_md: Name the three kinds of joint classified by the amount of movement and give one place in the body where each is found.

answer.model_answer_md: **Immovable** joints allow no movement and are found between the bones of the skull. **Slightly movable** joints allow a small movement and are found between the vertebrae. **Freely movable** joints allow a wide range of movement and are found at the shoulder, elbow, hip or knee.

questions.solution_md: Immovable: skull; slightly movable: vertebrae; freely movable: shoulder or knee.

questions.stem_md: Compare a pivot joint and a gliding joint in respect of (i) movement, (ii) an example and (iii) one bone or set of bones involved.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) A **pivot joint** allows **rotation** of one bone round another; a **gliding joint** allows small **sliding** movements. (ii) Pivot: the **neck**; gliding: the **wrist** or **ankle**. (iii) Pivot: the **atlas and axis**; gliding: the **carpals** (or tarsals).

questions.solution_md: Rotation or sliding; neck or wrist; atlas and axis or carpals.

questions.stem_md:
A hospital has X-ray films of a skull, a rib cage and a backbone.

(a) Name the organ that each of these three structures protects. [3]

(b) State two other functions of the skeleton, with an example of each. [2]

(c) A child has a low number of red blood cells. Name the soft tissue in the bones that makes them and state the two minerals that the bones store. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the rib cage with the sternum and the vertebral column, naming four parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The skull protects the **brain**; the rib cage protects the **heart and lungs**; the backbone protects the **spinal cord**.

**(b)** Any two: **support** (holds the body upright and gives it shape); **movement** (muscles pull on the bones, which act as levers); **attachment of muscles**.

**(c)** **Red bone marrow** makes blood cells; bones store **calcium** and **phosphorus**.

**(d)** A **sternum** in the middle, **ribs** curving round from the **thoracic vertebrae** of the **vertebral column**; four labels.

questions.solution_md: Brain; heart and lungs; spinal cord; two other functions; red bone marrow, calcium and phosphorus; labelled rib cage.

questions.stem_md:
Study the diagram of the human skeleton. Parts are lettered A to E.

(a) Name the parts A, B and C. [3]

(b) Classify the parts D and E as axial or appendicular, and name D. [2]

(c) Each upper limb has 30 bones. Calculate the bones in both upper limbs, and the phalanges in both hands if each hand has 14. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the bones of one lower limb, naming four bones. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A is the **skull**, B is the **rib cage** (ribs) and C is the **vertebral column**.

**(b)** D is the **pelvic girdle** (hip bones) and E is the **femur**; **both are appendicular**.

**(c)** 2 × 30 = **60** bones; 2 × 14 = **28** phalanges.

**(d)** The **femur**, then the **patella** at the knee, the **tibia** and **fibula** side by side and the **bones of the foot**; four labels.

questions.solution_md: Skull, ribs, vertebral column; pelvic girdle, femur, appendicular; 60 and 28; labelled lower limb.

questions.stem_md:
Study the diagram of the vertebral column. Regions are lettered A to E.

(a) Name the regions A, B and C and state the number of vertebrae in each. [3]

(b) Name the parts D and E and explain why each is a single bone in an adult. [2]

(c) A child has 33 vertebrae. State the number of bones in the adult column and show how the number falls. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the rib cage with the sternum, naming four parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A is the **cervical** region (**7**), B the **thoracic** (**12**) and C the **lumbar** (**5**).

**(b)** D is the **sacrum** and E the **coccyx**; each is formed by **fused vertebrae** (five and four).

**(c)** The adult column has **26** bones: 24 separate vertebrae + 1 sacrum + 1 coccyx, because 9 vertebrae fuse into two bones.

**(d)** A **sternum** in the middle with **ribs** curving round from the back; the **true ribs** joined to the sternum and the **floating ribs** free; four labels.

questions.solution_md: Cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5; sacrum and coccyx fused; 26 bones; labelled rib cage.

Study the diagram of four freely movable joints. They are lettered A to D.

(a) Name the joints A, B and C. [3]

(b) Give one place in the body where each of A and B is found. [2]

(c) State the movement allowed by C and by D. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the joint A, naming three parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A is a **ball and socket** joint, B a **hinge** joint and C a **pivot** joint.

**(b)** A: the **shoulder** or **hip**; B: the **elbow** or **knee**.

**(c)** C allows **rotation** of one bone round another; D (a gliding joint) allows small **sliding** movements.

**(d)** A **rounded head** of one bone fitting into the **cup (socket)** of the other, with **cartilage**, **synovial fluid** or **ligaments** shown; three labels.

questions.solution_md: Ball and socket, hinge, pivot; shoulder and elbow; rotation and sliding; labelled joint.

questions.stem_md:
A gymnast swings her arm round in a full circle, bends her knee and turns her head to look behind her.

(a) Name the joint at the shoulder and the kind of movement that makes the full circle possible. [2]

(b) Name the joint at the knee and state how its movement differs from that at the shoulder. [2]

(c) Name the joint that turns the head and the two bones that form it. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the joint at her knee, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A **ball and socket** joint; it moves in **all directions** and can **rotate**.

**(b)** A **hinge** joint; it moves in **one plane only** (back and forth), not in all directions.

**(c)** A **pivot** joint between the **atlas** and the **axis**.

**(d)** The **femur** and **tibia** meeting at the knee with **cartilage** on the bone ends, **synovial fluid** in a capsule and **ligaments**; the **direction of movement** shown by an arrow; four labels.

questions.solution_md: Ball and socket, all directions; hinge, one plane; pivot, atlas and axis; labelled hinge joint.

questions.stem_md:
A robot designer builds a model arm with hinge joints at the shoulder, elbow and wrist and claims that it can move exactly like a human arm.

(a) Name the kind of joint found in a human shoulder and in a human wrist. [2]

(b) State one movement that a human can make at the shoulder which the hinge joint of the model cannot. [2]

(c) Suggest which kind of joint the designer should use at the shoulder and give a reason. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the bones of one human upper limb, naming four bones. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The shoulder is a **ball and socket** joint; the wrist has **gliding** joints.

**(b)** A hinge moves in one plane only. A human can **swing the arm in a full circle** or **rotate it** at the shoulder, in **all directions**, which a hinge cannot do.

**(c)** A **ball and socket** joint, because it allows movement in **all directions** and rotation, as in the human shoulder.

**(d)** **Humerus**, then **radius and ulna** side by side, then **carpals, metacarpals and phalanges** of the hand; four labels.

questions.solution_md: Ball and socket; gliding; rotation in all directions; ball and socket at the shoulder; labelled arm bones.
